title: Rumpelstiltskin
paragraphs: Beside a wood, in a country far away, a fine stream flowed, and on the stream stood a mill. The miller’s house was close by, and the miller, as you should know, had a very beautiful daughter. She was also sharp and clever, and the miller was so proud of her that one day he told the king of that land, who often came to hunt in the wood, that his daughter could spin straw into gold. Now this king loved money, and when he heard the miller’s boast, his greed was stirred and he had the girl brought to him. He led her to a room in his palace that held a huge heap of straw, gave her a spinning-wheel, and said, “All of this must be spun into gold by morning, if you value your life.” The poor girl pleaded that it was only a foolish boast of her father’s and that she could do no such thing as spin straw into gold. It made no difference: the door was locked, and she was left alone.

She sat down in a corner of the room and began to lament her cruel fate. Suddenly the door opened and a comical little man hobbled in. “Good morning to you, my girl,” he said. “Why are you crying?” “Oh,” she said, “I have to spin this straw into gold, and I don’t know how.” “What will you give me,” said the hobgoblin, “if I do it for you?” “My necklace,” the girl replied. He took her up on it, sat down at the wheel, and whistled and sang:

“Round about, round about,
Lo and behold!
Reel away, reel away,
Straw into gold!”
And the wheel went merrily round and round. The work was soon finished, and all the straw was spun into gold.

When the king came and saw it, he was amazed and delighted, but it only made him hungrier for gold. He shut the miller’s poor daughter in again with a new task. She had no idea what to do and sat down to weep once more, but soon the dwarf opened the door and said, “What will you give me to do your task?” “The ring on my finger,” she said. So her little friend took the ring and set to work at the wheel again, whistling and singing:

“Turn and turn, turn and turn,
Watch it now unfold!
Spin away, spin away,
Straw becomes gold!”
until, well before morning, everything was done again.

The king was overjoyed to see all that glittering treasure, but he still wanted more. He took the miller’s daughter to an even bigger heap and said, “All this must be spun tonight, and if it is, you will be my queen.” As soon as she was alone, the dwarf came in and said, “What will you give me to spin gold for you this third time?” “I have nothing left,” she said. “Then promise me,” said the little man, “that you will give me the first child you have once you are queen.” “That may never happen,” thought the miller’s daughter, and since she knew no other way to get the task done, she promised what he asked. Round went the wheel again to the same old song, and the manikin once more spun the heap into gold. In the morning the king came and found everything he wanted. He had to keep his word, so he married the miller’s daughter, and she truly became queen.

When her first child was born she was very happy, and she forgot all about the dwarf and what she had promised. But one day he came into her room, where she sat playing with her baby, and reminded her. She was bitterly distressed and offered him all the wealth of the kingdom if he would release her, but it was no use. At last her tears softened him, and he said, “I will give you three days. If you can tell me my name in that time, you may keep your child.”

The queen lay awake all that night, thinking of every odd name she had ever heard, and she sent messengers all over the land to find new ones. The next day the little man came, and she started with TIMOTHY, ICHABOD, BENJAMIN, JEREMIAH, and every other name she could remember. To each and every one he replied, “Madam, that is not my name.”

On the second day she began with all the funny names she could find, BANDY-LEGS, HUNCHBACK, CROOK-SHANKS, and so on. But the little gentleman still answered every one of them, “Madam, that is not my name.”

On the third day one of the messengers came back and said, “I have traveled for two days without hearing of any other names. But yesterday, as I was climbing a high hill, in the forest where the fox and the hare say good night to each other, I saw a little hut. In front of the hut a fire was burning, and around the fire a funny little dwarf was dancing on one leg and singing:

“Merrily the feast I’ll make.
Today I’ll brew, tomorrow bake;
Merrily I’ll dance and sing,
For the next day a stranger will bring.
Little does my lady dream
Rumpelstiltskin is my name!”

When the queen heard this she jumped for joy. As soon as her little friend arrived, she sat on her throne and called her whole court around to enjoy the fun. The nurse stood beside her with the baby in her arms, as though it were all ready to be handed over. The little man began to chuckle at the thought of taking the poor child home to his hut in the woods, and he cried, “Now, lady, what is my name?” “Is it JOHN?” she asked. “No, madam!” “Is it TOM?” “No, madam!” “Is it JEMMY?” “It is not.” “Could your name be RUMPELSTILTSKIN?” said the lady slyly. “A witch told you that!—a witch told you that!” shrieked the little man, and in his rage he stamped his right foot so deep into the floor that he had to grab it with both hands to pull it out.

Then he made off as fast as he could, while the nurse laughed and the baby crowed. The whole court jeered at him for going to so much trouble for nothing, and called, “We wish you a very good morning and a merry feast, Mr RUMPLESTILTSKIN!”
